title: Uganda says it vaccinated 8.28 million children against measles and rubella. The next test is who was missed.
subtitle: The five-day campaign exceeded its operational target, but district results, reconciled registers and independent checks are still needed to show whether protection reached every community.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Originally reported 4 October 2026; updated with the post-campaign result announced 6 October 2026.

Uganda says its five-day measles–rubella campaign recorded 8,285,835 vaccinations among children aged nine to 59 months, exceeding the operational target set before teams began work on 1 October. The headline number is an important public-health achievement. It is also the beginning of the accountability work, not the end of it.

The Ministry of Health announced the total after the campaign closed on 5 October and credited health workers, parents, caregivers, community leaders and development partners. It urged families to continue routine immunisation, because the additional campaign dose does not replace the scheduled measles–rubella doses at nine and 18 months or any other vaccine a child may have missed.

The result is higher than both the earlier operational target of about 7.47 million children and the pre-campaign estimate of 7,864,794 eligible children. That does not by itself prove duplication or error. Population projections can undercount rapidly growing or mobile communities, children may cross administrative boundaries, and campaign registers can capture children missed by older estimates. But a total above the estimated eligible population makes independent coverage checks, record cleaning and district-level reporting especially important.

Administrative totals count recorded doses. They do not automatically show whether 95% of children were reached in every district, whether the same child appeared in more than one register, or which communities remained below the threshold needed to interrupt measles transmission.
Parents were willing. Services still had to reach them.

Before the campaign, WHO, the Ministry of Health, UNICEF and research partners surveyed nearly 1,900 caregivers across rural, urban, island, refugee-hosting and pastoralist communities. Almost 93% of rural respondents said they intended to vaccinate their children fully, 99% said they knew where vaccination was available and 96% reported encouragement from relatives, friends or community leaders.

The public summary did not provide enough information about sampling, question wording or subgroup results to treat those percentages as a national poll. Intentions reported in a survey are also not the same as documented vaccination. Even so, the findings challenge the convenient claim that missed doses are mainly caused by indifferent parents.

Distance, transport costs, inconvenient clinic hours, uncertain vaccine supply, mobile livelihoods and the unpaid time required for another visit can keep a willing family away. Mothers often carry the work of coordinating those visits, but a missed dose should not be treated automatically as a mother’s personal failure. Health services decide where teams are placed, whether a working parent can use them, whether records follow a displaced child and whether someone returns after the campaign ends.
Uganda starts protection more successfully than it completes it

Uganda introduced the combined measles–rubella vaccine into routine immunisation in October 2019 and added a second routine dose in October 2022. Ministry figures reported before the campaign placed first-dose coverage at 92% in 2025, down from 95% in 2023. Second-dose coverage was only 64%, and WHO said just 21 of 146 districts reached the required second-dose target in 2025.

The measures are not interchangeable. A national percentage can conceal districts with much lower access, while a count of districts does not show how many children live in each one. Together, however, they show that Uganda has been substantially better at beginning measles protection than completing it.

WHO estimated that approximately three million children missed their second dose during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Catch-up work later reached about 1.5 million. That does not mean exactly 1.5 million remained unprotected, because children age into and out of target groups, migrate, receive vaccines through other routes or lack complete records. It does show why a national campaign was considered necessary.

Uganda confirmed 66 measles outbreaks in 2025, according to WHO. Among confirmed cases investigated, 64% had never received a measles vaccine and none had received both recommended doses. In a review of deaths in Moroto and Napak districts, 92% of the children who died had never been vaccinated.

Those figures describe identified cases and reviewed deaths, not the risk faced by every unvaccinated child. Nutrition, delayed treatment and access to clinical care can also affect whether a child survives. They nevertheless show why measles cannot be dismissed as an ordinary rash. The disease can cause pneumonia, severe diarrhoea, dehydration, blindness, brain inflammation and death.
Rubella makes this a women’s-health story too

Rubella is often mild in a child or adult, but infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, fetal death or congenital rubella syndrome, with possible damage to hearing, sight, the heart and the brain. Reducing transmission therefore protects more than the child receiving the injection; it also reduces exposure for pregnant women and future pregnancies.

The campaign was non-selective: eligibility was based on age rather than the vaccination history written on a child’s card. An additional dose was intentional and designed to close immunity gaps quickly, including where earlier records were missing or a previous dose did not produce adequate protection.

Officials advised caregivers to remain at the vaccination point for about 30 minutes so health workers could observe children for an immediate reaction. Mild fever, soreness or rash can occur and usually resolves. Serious reactions are rare, but a credible immunisation programme should record, investigate and publicly report suspected adverse events rather than treating questions as opposition.
A national total can hide local vulnerability

Measles spreads so efficiently that high national coverage can coexist with local outbreaks. The benchmark is at least 95% coverage with two doses in every community, not simply a national average. Reaching the target overall while leaving an island, refugee settlement, pastoralist community or crowded urban neighbourhood far below it preserves a pocket in which the virus can spread.

The ministry’s 8.28-million total should therefore be followed by district results, the number of children reached outside fixed facilities, reconciled registers, stock and staffing reports, adverse-event data and an independent post-campaign coverage survey. Those checks can distinguish an impressive mobilisation from durable, evenly distributed protection.

The campaign was supported by Gavi, WHO, UNICEF and other partners. That partnership made a five-day operation possible, but emergency campaigns cannot substitute indefinitely for routine services. A dose delivered in October protects a child now. A reliable system must also be ready for the child born in November, the family that moves and the mother who cannot leave work during clinic hours.

Uganda’s reported result shows what public mobilisation can achieve. The next question is whether the health system can identify the children who remain unprotected, return for them and keep them connected to routine care long after the campaign tents are folded.
The Athena Perspective.
